The first link is the less direct one: in married couples, a warm and tender disposition (trait expressiveness) predicts both affectionate behavior and idealization of the partner (Miller et al., 2003). The second link is better documented. Partners recognize the nonverbal display of love, and this display accompanies commitment-enhancing behavior (Gonzaga et al., 2001). Declaring love communicates an intention to commit (Ackerman et al., 2011). Acts that reveal love make rivals less interested in the actor (Gelbart et al., 2025), and relationships made visible on social media are perceived as more committed (Emery et al., 2015). To the extent that idealization feeds these expressions, it feeds signals of commitment.

Answers to an anonymous survey are not signals. But dispositions shaped by their benefits of reciprocity and reputation do not switch off when no one is watching (for instance, people are generous in anonymous one-shot interactions; Delton et al., 2011; and they punish unfair behavior when their punishment cannot be seen; Jordan & Rand, 2020). Anonymous answers can therefore reflect the motivation that produces signals, even though they are not signals themselves.

We therefore use the endorsement of idealizing statements as an indirect measure of the motivation behind romantic signaling, not as a measure of signaling itself. If the value of signaling commitment declines with development, the endorsement of idealizing statements should decline too, relative to statements that describe the relationship without idealizing it. Study 3 tests this implication. It does not actually test whether respondents send fewer signals to their partners.

To test our hypothesis, we reanalyzed the cross-national dataset of Sorokowski and colleagues (2023), in which participants answered the 45 items of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale. The items describe emotions, cognitions, and behaviors related to romantic relationships. The analytic sample included 388,840 item-level responses from 8,792 participants in 45 countries (see Methods for exclusions).

Crucially for our purposes, these items vary widely in their degree of partner idealization. Some items strongly imply idealization and exclusivity (e.g., "Nothing is more important to me than my relationship"), others involve moderate idealization (e.g., "I find my partner very personally attractive"), and still others involve no idealization at all (e.g., "I give considerable emotional support to my partner"). Rather than aggregating items into the traditional dimensions of passion, intimacy, and commitment, we treated partner idealization as a continuous item-level property. This decision follows directly from the model. Since the predicted decline reflects signaling rather than romantic experience as a whole, it should be detectable at the item level, where signaling content varies.

Four independent coders (three authors blind to the distribution of the data, one coder blind to the hypothesis) rated each of the 45 items for their level of partner idealization. The reliability of the averaged rating was high (ICC(2,k) = 0.875). Ratings were averaged to yield a single partner idealization score per item.

Before turning to the model, Figure 3A shows the pattern at the country level. We split the 45 items at the median partner idealization score (0.25) and computed, for each country, the mean endorsement of the 24 high-idealization items and of the 21 low-idealization items. Endorsement of both groups of items is higher in moderately developed countries than in the least developed ones. It levels off earlier, and falls further, for high-idealization items (e.g., "Nothing is more important to me than my relationship") than for low-idealization items (e.g., "I give considerable emotional support to my partner"): quadratic fits across countries peak at an HDI of 0.79 for high-idealization items and 0.86 for low-idealization items. The gap between the two groups therefore widens with HDI (r = 0.58 across the 45 countries). These country means describe the pattern but do not test it: they combine development with other differences between countries, and they depend on how respondents in each country use the rating scale. The analyses below test the pattern on each participant's answers.

To test this pattern, we used the continuous variation in PI across all 45 items. As pre-registered, we modeled each participant's response to each item (388,840 responses from 8,792 participants in 45 countries) as a function of the item's PI score, the HDI of the participant's country, the participant's SES, and their interactions, with random intercepts for participant, item, and country (model M0, pre-registered; see Methods for the full specification). Following the preregistration, a prediction was supported if the 95% interval of a bootstrap excluded zero; because HDI varies between countries only, the bootstrap resampled countries. The PI × HDI interaction combines a property of items with a property of countries. We therefore also report a model that lets the effect of PI vary across countries and across participants (model M1, not preregistered; added during revision in response to a reviewer's suggestion), so that the interaction is tested against the variation between countries.

The key prediction is that the association between development and endorsement depends on how idealizing the item is. This is captured by the PI × HDI interaction. As predicted, this interaction was negative: the more an item implies partner idealization, the lower its endorsement in more developed countries, relative to the other items (M0: b = -0.048, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.061, -0.028]; M1: b = -0.050, 95% CI [-0.072, -0.027], t(42.4) = -4.43, p < .001). The pre-registered prediction for SES was not supported: the PI × SES interaction was negative, but its bootstrap interval included zero (M0: b = -0.007, 95% CI [-0.015, 0.001]). In M1, which does not let this interaction vary between countries, it was significant (b = -0.010, 95% CI [-0.015, -0.005], t(8,741) = -4.14, p < .001). This association was present within countries: participants who rated their economic situation higher than others in their country endorsed idealizing items relatively less (Supplementary Note 4).

Development was not associated with a uniform change in endorsement. The quadratic term of HDI was negative (M0: b = -0.056, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.088, -0.015]), and it applies to all items: the pre-registered model has a single curvature, which the PI × HDI interaction shifts according to how idealizing the item is. The implied slope of endorsement on HDI (in SD units) therefore crosses zero at a lower HDI for idealizing items. In M1, for the most idealizing item, it is 0.19 at an HDI of 0.55, -0.02 at 0.75 and -0.24 (SE = 0.06) at 0.95, but for the least idealizing item, it is 0.37, 0.15 and -0.07 (SE = 0.05). At the highest levels of development, endorsement thus declines for strongly idealizing items and does not change reliably for items without idealization. The interaction of PI with squared HDI, added to M1, was close to zero (b = 0.002, p = .843). Additional covariates (age, gender, relationship length), and the interactions of gender and relationship length with PI, are reported in Supplementary Table S5. The outcome and the continuous predictors are z-scored. Reference category for gender: man. Full coefficients in Supplementary Table S5.

The rise and fall of the country means of this survey may partly reflect differences in how respondents use rating scales rather than differences in love (Ulitzsch et al., 2024; for a reply, see Sorokowski & Kowal, 2024). Such differences could also produce the PI × HDI interaction, even if they affected all items equally. Extreme responding stretches answers away from the midpoint, which widens the distance between items, while the top of the scale compresses the answers to items already close to it, which narrows it. The gap between idealizing and other items could therefore change with HDI if extreme responding differed between more and less developed countries, all the more so if idealizing items, often phrased in absolute terms, were the most sensitive to it. We tested this in three ways (Supplementary Note 4). First, across countries, extreme responding was not associated with HDI, whether measured by the share of answers at the top of the scale (r = 0.22, p = .146) or with a multi-process item response model (r = 0.16, p = .298; Böckenholt & Meiser, 2017). In this model, idealizing items were less sensitive to extreme responding than other items, not more (r = -0.34 across the 45 items, p = .022). Second, controlling for response style did not weaken the interaction (b from -0.048 to -0.054, all p < .001, against -0.050 without these controls), whether it was measured by each participant's or each country's share of answers at the top of the scale or at either end of it, or by the multi-process model. Third, the interaction remained when each participant's answers were centered, standardized or ranked within participant (t from -4.19 to -5.63, all p < .001, against -4.16 for the raw answers of the same participants). Centering removes differences in the overall level of a participant's answers, standardizing also removes differences in their spread, and ranking keeps only their order. Differences in scale use therefore do not account for the interaction, at least in the forms that these data allow us to measure. Some countries depart from this pattern. Supplementary Table S7 gives, for each country, the gap between low-and high-idealization items and its departure from the linear trend in HDI. Among the most developed countries, the gap is larger than the trend predicts in Austria (+0.48 points) and Germany (+0.33), and smaller in the United States (-0.16), the Netherlands (-0.16) and Spain (-0.13); Sweden, Belgium, Norway, and Australia are close to the trend. Departures of similar size occur at intermediate levels of development (Jordan, -0.58; Uruguay, +0.46; Malaysia, -0.41). The model's theoretical variable is the prevalence of long-term commitment, and interpersonal trust differs between equally developed countries (Delhey & Newton, 2005). We therefore tested trust directly, using the share of respondents who say that most people can be trusted (Integrated Values Surveys, 2024; 41 countries). Trust predicted the idealization slope when it replaced HDI in M1 (b = -0.030, p = .013), but not when both entered the model (b = -0.009, p = .453), whereas HDI remained (b = -0.046, p = .004). In these data, HDI is a better predictor (Supplementary Note 4).

These results are consistent with the model's prediction. Development is not associated with a uniform decline in endorsement, but with a lower endorsement of idealizing statements relative to the other items. These results suggest that the decline of romantic love reported in this survey at the highest levels of development concerns its idealizing expressions more than the motivation to sustain a relationship.

Study 4: Socio-economic development predicts lower infidelity

A central claim of the model is that the value of romantic signaling depends nonlinearly on the prevalence of long-term commitment in the population. When defection is common, even highly committed individuals must signal to avoid being mistaken for opportunistic types, because choosers cannot safely assume commitment in the absence of explicit reassurance. By contrast, once a sufficiently large share of individuals reliably sustain long-term exclusive cooperation, the informational environment changes. At that point, choosers can reasonably treat non-signaling as evidence of commitment rather than as a risk, allowing highly cooperative individuals to refrain from signaling without incurring coordination costs. In this sense, the decline of romantic signaling requires that long-term commitment be common enough for trust to become the default.

Study 4 tests the first step of this argument: whether socio-economic development is associated with lower rates of infidelity. We use the prevalence of fidelity within a society as an indicator of how common long-term commitment is. The study does not test the level of fidelity at which signaling changes.

We use cross-national survey data (Kowal et al., 2025) in which participants answered the question: "Have you ever been sexually or emotionally unfaithful to a romantic partner?" The question covers the whole life, not only the current relationship; answers were coded 1 (yes) or 0 (no). Country-level socio-economic development was operationalized using the Human Development Index (HDI) of 2021, the year of data collection. The analytic sample included 84,382 participants nested within 160 countries (see Methods for exclusions and preprocessing).

At the country level, the share of respondents reporting any infidelity decreased with HDI across the 160 countries (Pearson r = -0.16, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.01], p = .040). This correlation gives each country the same weight, although countries contributed between 1 and 8,466 respondents. Weighted by the number of respondents, the association was close to zero (r = -0.07, p = .373), with the five largest samples carrying 31% of the weight. Among the 82 countries with at least 50 respondents, r = -0.27 (95% CI [-0.46, -0.06], p = .012). The country-level association therefore depends on how countries are weighted. The multilevel model below does not require choosing weights: countries with few respondents count little, and the largest samples do not dominate.

The individual-level analysis uses all 84,382 participants and models the variation between countries. In a multilevel logistic regression with a random intercept for country (σ² = 0.27, SD = 0.52, n = 84,382 individuals nested within 160 countries), the focal effect of HDI was negative and significant on the log-odds of reporting any infidelity (β = -0.13, SE = 0.04, z = -3.24, p = .001; standardized), corresponding to an odds ratio of OR = 0.88, 95% CI [0.81, 0.95] per onestandard-deviation increase in HDI. Controlling for age (β = 0.33, z = 40.30, p < .001), individual SES (β = 0.04, z = 4.70, p < .001), and gender (women vs men: β = -0.10, z = -6.10, p < .001) did not alter the direction or significance of the focal effect. Age was by far the strongest individual-level predictor, with older participants reporting more lifetime infidelity, as expected from cumulative exposure. Importantly, individual SES displayed the opposite sign to HDI (positive rather than negative), indicating that the country-level association is not explained by individual social class. The association held among participants under 65 and with GDP per capita in place of HDI. It was clear among men (β = -0.23, z = -4.97, p < .001) but not among women (β = -0.06, z = -1.40, p = .162; Supplementary Note 5).

Together, these results show that reported infidelity is lower in more developed countries, in parallel with the pattern documented in Study 3. In more developed countries, people are not only more selective in which items of a love scale they endorse: they are also less likely to report having been unfaithful. Both findings are consistent with the model, although neither measures signals of commitment directly.

Discussion

The present work addressed a paradox at the intersection of evolutionary psychology, cultural change, and romantic behavior: why do expressions of romantic love peak and then decline in the most socio-economically developed societies, precisely where long-term commitment should be most advantageous? We proposed that this pattern does not reflect a weakening of pairbonding motivations, but a shift in the adaptive value of romantic signals: when long-term commitment becomes sufficiently prevalent, overt signaling becomes unnecessary and even counterproductive, because it reveals an expectation that the relationship requires reassurance. Three studies tested indirect implications of this account.

A related logic appears in earlier models. In countersignaling models (Feltovich et al., 2002; Harbaugh & To, 2020), high types stay silent because receivers have access to additional information about them; signaling would then reveal a lack of confidence in this information. In the signal-burying model (Hoffman et al., 2018), high types pay the cost of a signal but conceal it, either because they expect their concealed signal to be revealed anyway, or because they prefer to be noticed only by receivers who care about distinguishing them from medium types. In both classes of model, what makes high types' behavior informative is the existence of an additional, observable source of information, or assumed differences in how different receiver and sender types value each other. Our model relies on a different mechanism: silence is informative because it reveals beliefs about the match itself, and these beliefs are correlated with type through assortment alone.

Socio-economic development predicts lower rates of infidelity, consistent with the first condition of the model: long-term commitment is more common in more developed societies. Development is also associated with a selective attenuation of idealizing expressions of love, while non-idealizing components such as emotional support and relational care change little at the highest levels of development.

An important implication of our account is that romantic signals do not merely lose relevance in affluent societies: they can become actively aversive. In high-trust environments, overt signaling may downgrade the perceived relationship by implying that reassurance is still required and longterm commitment is not secured. What might otherwise be interpreted as confidence and stability becomes reclassified as insecurity or short-termism. This reclassification carries an opportunity cost: it forecloses access to a high-trust, low-maintenance form of cooperation. This logic may also explain why reactions to overt romance have changed in kind, and not only in frequency. If romantic love were simply less necessary, one would expect indifference. Instead, overt romantic displays often elicit discomfort or embarrassment, at least among the educated, affluent groups in which this reaction has been described (Eco, 1983 (Eco, /1984;; Illouz, 1997; Swidler, 2001), and romance itself has become an object of irony. Studying Hollywood romance films, Dowd and Pallotta (2000) noted that in the 1990s romance 'faces the challenge of the new forces of postmodern irony and disbelief' (p. 563). Our model does not represent emotions, but it suggests why such reactions arise. When long-term commitment is common, signals need not merely lose their value; they can convey unfavorable information, as in the aversive signaling equilibrium. In this equilibrium, high-trust partners expect deep commitment, and deeply committed individuals expect high-trust partners. A signal instead reveals someone capable only of more limited cooperation, overturning the high-trust partner's expectation of deep commitment. A grand declaration can therefore place those who witness it, including the partner, in a dilemma. If they let it pass, they conceal their judgment and leave the sender exposed; if they react, they make the sender lose face. Goffman (1956) traced embarrassment to this kind of situation, in which a person claims an image that others cannot ratify, and showed that witnesses share it (see also Krach et al., 2011, on vicarious embarrassment). Irony offers a way out. By quoting a declaration rather than making it, as in Eco's example, a person can express attachment while showing that they know the gesture is excessive.

Our account also differs from sociological explanations of the same shift. Giddens (1992) described the decline of romantic love, built around a unique and idealized partner, and the rise of "confluent love" and of the "pure relationship" (i.e., a relationship negotiated between equals, sustained by mutual disclosure, and lasting as long as it satisfies both partners). He saw romantic ideals fragment "under the pressure of female sexual emancipation and autonomy" (p. 61). His account and ours agree on what declines: as confluent love spreads, "the finding of a 'special person' recedes" (p. 62). They differ in two ways. The first is the mechanism. In his account, idealized love declines because women come to expect equality within the relationship, whereas romantic love "has always been imbalanced in gender terms" (p. 62). In ours, it declines because signaling commitment becomes less useful, and even counterproductive, when long-term commitment is more common.

The second is commitment itself. A pure relationship lasts only "until further notice" (p. 63), whereas our account assumes that long-term commitment becomes more common. Studies of couples have questioned this point: the couples they describe sought relationships intended to last (Jamieson, 1999), and couple relationships appear less contingent than the pure relationship implies (Smart, 2007). The two mechanisms are not exclusive. When women no longer depend on their partner's resources, a misplaced commitment costs less, and signals of commitment may matter less. Our data cannot separate them, because gender equality and human development are strongly correlated across countries. Other accounts attribute the retreat of idealized romance to broader cultural changes, such as the commodification of emotional life (Illouz, 2012 (Illouz, , 2019) ) or the weakening of social bonds in late modernity (Bauman, 2003). These accounts predict a more general erosion of romantic attachment, yet in Study 3 endorsement of non-idealizing items did not decline reliably at the highest levels of development.

Our model also explains something that Giddens cannot account for: he described romantic love as "essentially feminised love" (p. 43) yet men endorse idealizing statements more than women do (Study 3) and are more likely to say "I love you" first (Ackerman et al., 2011; Watkins et al., 2022). This is expected if signals of commitment are sent to the partner who bears the higher cost of a misplaced commitment, historically women (Ackerman et al., 2011). Our account also makes a prediction that his does not: the same overt romantic gesture should be read as a sign of commitment where long-term commitment is rare, but as a sign of doubt about the relationship where it is common.

Note that these sources do not date the change in the same way. Love themes declined in U.S. top-40 lyrics after the 1970s (Madanikia & Bartholomew, 2014), Giddens (1992) described the new ideal by the early 1990s, and romantic content in U.S. films peaked in the early-to-mid 2000s (Study 1). We do not expect these dates to coincide. Media address different audiences, the corpora and measures differ, and qualitative sociology tends to detect changes in norms when they begin, often in small and relatively privileged groups, before they appear in aggregate data. These sources agree on the direction of the change, not on its timing. Which medium leads, and which groups change first, could be tested with corpora dated at the level of the year and of the audience.

More broadly, these findings illustrate how ecological changes can alter the meaning of signals without altering their form. Romantic gestures, declarations, and idealization cues may persist, but their interpretation depends on background levels of trust. As environments become safer and cooperation more reliable, the same behaviors can reverse their informational valence. This logic likely extends beyond romantic relationships. Many domains of social life, from gift-giving to moral grandstanding, rely on signals whose value depends on background uncertainty. When trust is scarce, signals stabilize cooperation. When trust is abundant, signals can crowd out deeper forms of cooperation (Feltovich et al., 2002; Harbaugh & To, 2020). Romantic love offers a particularly clear case because the stakes of miscoordination are high and the signals are salient.

Several limitations warrant discussion. First, while we used multiple converging methods, our infidelity measure relies on self-report and may be affected by social desirability biases. However, such biases would need to vary systematically with HDI in a way that mimics the model's predictions, which seems unlikely. Second, Study 3 measures the endorsement of idealizing statements, not signals. Idealization also has private benefits, such as sustaining satisfaction in the relationship (Murray et al., 1996 (Murray et al., , 2011)). If these benefits were larger where relationships are less secure, they would predict the same pattern as the signaling account, and our data cannot separate the two. Future work could measure signals directly, such as public declarations, costly gifts, or social media displays. Third, Study 1 relies on a language model's ratings, without independent human coding of film content. The rise and fall of the share of Romance-tagged films, a label assigned by IMDb rather than by the model, partly addresses this concern, but it measures genre, not the romantic content of each film. Fourth, we only focus on country-level variations in ecological variables: future research could examine within-society variation in trust environments, for instance across neighborhoods. Finally, our evidence remains correlational. Although the convergence of cross-national, diachronic, and item-level patterns is consistent with the proposed signaling mechanism, direct experimental tests are needed to establish causality. Future work could manipulate trust environments and signal intensity in vignette or behavioral paradigms to test whether romantic signals indeed lose their reassuring function and acquire a counterproductive one when commitment is taken for granted.

More broadly, the same logic may extend to non-romantic forms of socialization. Many social bonds (e.g., friendships, kinship ties, patron-client relationships, professional alliances) are sustained by expressions of loyalty, devotion, or affection that function, at least in part, as costly signals of commitment. Cross-cultural variation in these expressions may follow the same logic. In societies with tightly knit kinship, where people trust their in-group much more than strangers, cooperation relies more on communal moral values such as in-group loyalty (Enke, 2019). Married couples exchange gifts more often in the United States, where divorce is more frequent, than in Japan (Komiya et al., 2019). Our framework may explain these patterns: when background institutions and reputational systems make defection costly and cooperation predictable, overt signals of loyalty lose their informational function and may even signal that the relationship requires reassurance. The decline of overt romantic signaling in affluent societies may thus be one instance of a broader phenomenon in which high-trust environments selectively suppress the expressive forms of cooperation while preserving its substantive content.

Taken together, the present findings are consistent with a hypothesis for an apparent evolutionary paradox: romantic love may fade in developed societies not because bonds are weaker, but because they are more secure. As long-term commitment becomes common, reassurance becomes unnecessary, and signaling becomes costly. Love, in this sense, becomes quieter, not because it matters less, but because it can be taken for granted.

Method

Study 1

Dataset

We selected all films in the film database with the United States as their Wikidata country of origin and a release year after 1970. The database merges IMDb records, each with at least 99 user votes, with Wikidata and Wikipedia. The corpus contains 13,415 feature films released in 1971-2020 (the last year is incomplete in the source database and contributes 6 films only). It was deposited on OSF with the pre-registration on March 24, 2024 (https://osf.io/84k6w/); the analyzed file has identical metadata. Apocalypse Now (1979) appears twice. Both rows were kept; removing the duplicate does not change the results.

Measures

Following the protocol of Dubourg et al. (2024), we obtained annotations of two love-related constructs for every film: a broad General Love Score and a stricter Romantic Love Score (the primary outcome). Annotations were collected in spring 2024, after the pre-registration, through the OpenAI API at a temperature of 0. The model alias "gpt-4" is gpt-4-0613, with training data up to September 2021. Each film received one call per construct. The prompts, reproduced below ([Title] replaced by the film title), supplied only the film title.

For General Love: "Rate the significance of love in each movie on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 represents a complete absence or irrelevance of love, and 10 indicates that love is central and extremely relevant. Focus exclusively on the presence and impact of love between partners, setting aside other forms of love or relationships such as familial bonds or friendships. Provide a very brief justification. You must write the score after / SCORE = / at the end, with no text nor symbol after. If you don't know the movie, score NA. The movie is: [Title]." For Romantic Love: "Romantic love is defined as an all-consuming type of love, which is unconditional and enduring, capable of overcoming challenges and standing the test of time. Rate the significance of romantic love in each movie on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 represents a complete absence or irrelevance of romantic love, and 10 indicates that romantic love is central and extremely relevant. Focus exclusively on the presence and impact of romantic love between partners, setting aside other forms of love or relationships such as familial bonds or friendships. Provide a very brief justification. You must write the score after / SCORE = / at the end, with no text nor symbol after. If you don't know the movie, score NA. The movie is: [Title]."

For each of the two annotations, the numeric score was parsed from the model's response using regular expressions. The accompanying justification was retained as the text preceding the SCORE marker. Films for which the LLM declined to rate (e.g., "I don't know this movie", or responses requesting disambiguation) were assigned a missing score. After parsing, a valid General Love score was available for 12,505 films (93.2 % of the corpus) and a valid Romantic Love score for 12,369 films (92.2 %). All subsequent analyses use these two analytic samples. The 1,046 films without a Romantic Love Score and the 910 without a General Love Score were excluded from the corresponding analyses only, and every release year from 1971 to 2020 remained represented.

Validity check

Each score was checked against the IMDb Romance genre tag using Welch's two-sample t-test (two-sided), comparing films tagged as Romance with other films. The pre-registration specified that temporal analyses would be conducted only if Romance-tagged films scored significantly higher on both outcomes (direction pre-specified). Failure would stop further hypothesis testing. Because IMDb information is probably part of the model's training data, the tag is not an independent ground truth. Passing the check shows that the scores track the genre label, not that they measure film content independently of it.

Statistical analysis

To test the pre-registered prediction of a decline of love across time (following Sorokowski et al., 2023), we fit four ordinary least squares regression models per outcome, consistent with the preregistered analysis plan: (M1) a linear model with release year as the sole predictor, (M2) a linear model additionally controlling for the number of films released in the same year (a production-volume control that includes films without a score), (M3) a quadratic model including both a linear and a squared year term, and (M4) a quadratic model with the production-volume control.

In all four models, release year was mean-centered and z-scored. The squared term was computed from standardized year and then z-scored. The production-volume control was also zscored. Outcomes kept their 0-10 scale, so coefficients represent score changes per SD of the predictor rather than fully standardized betas. The control counts all corpus films released that year, including films without scores, following the pre-registration (see SI for an alternative specification).

Model selection followed the pre-registered rule: we retained and interpreted the model with the lowest AIC. The pre-registered hypothesis was that (i) if a linear model was selected, the coefficient of year would be negative and significant, or (ii) if a quadratic model was selected, the coefficient of year² would be negative and significant. Inference was based on two-sided t-tests of the fixed effects, and 95 % confidence intervals were obtained from the model-based standard errors (no correction for multiple comparisons was applied because the two outcomes are treated as a primary pre-registered test and a replication, respectively). Analyses were conducted in R 4.5.1, and the scripts (study1_analysis.R, study1_robustness.R and study1_romance_tag.R) are available on OSF. Supplementary Note 2 lists implementation decisions that the pre-registration did not specify, and Supplementary Note 3 reports additional checks that were not preregistered: missing scores, film popularity, dependence among films released in the same year, and the shape of the curve.

Study 2

We develop a model of costly signaling in cooperative relationships, building on a framework in which cooperation serves as a signal of time preferences (Lie-Panis & André, 2022; Lie-Panis & Hilbe, 2026). Full details and derivations are provided in Supplementary Note 1.

Players

We consider a long-lived signaler matched with a short-lived chooser. The signaler's discount factor δ is privately known and takes one of three values: δL<δM<δH, corresponding to low, medium, and high-patience types, drawn with probabilities pL, pM, and pH. The chooser is either high-trust (probability qH) or low-trust (probability qL=1-qH).

Matching

With probability r, matching is assortative: high-patience signalers are paired with high-trust choosers, while other signalers are paired with low-trust choosers. With probability 1-r, matching is random. As a result, high-trust choosers hold more favorable prior beliefs about signaler patience than low-trust choosers.

Timing

The game has three phases. In Phase 1, the signaler privately observes their type and decides whether to pay cost k>0 to send a signal. In Phase 2, the signaler is matched with a chooser, who observes the signaling decision, permanently sets the level of cooperation-high or low-and decides whether to extend trust. In Phase 3, the signaler and chooser play an infinitely repeated trust game at the chosen level: in each round, the chooser decides whether to trust the signaler; if trusted, the signaler decides whether to reciprocate or cheat.

Cooperation levels

Cooperation can occur at two levels, reflected in trust game payoffs. At level l ∈ {L, H}, trust costs the chooser γl>0 and earns the signaler bl>0; reciprocation costs the signaler cl>0 and earns the chooser βl>0. Mutual cooperation is net beneficial for both players (γl<βl, cl<bl), and payoffs are larger at the high level (γL<γH, βL<βH, cL<cH, bL<bH).

Successful cooperation is more beneficial at the higher level for both players (bL-cL<bH-cH, βL-γL<βH-γH), but harder to sustain, with reciprocation requiring more patience (cL /bL<cH /bH) and trust requiring more favorable beliefs (γL /βL<γH /βH).

Other parameter assumptions

We assume that signaler types span both thresholds (δL<cL /bL<δM<cH /bH<δH), leading them to adopt different behaviors in equilibrium, with low-patience types cheating regardless of level or reputation, medium-patience types reciprocating at the low level and cheating at the high level, and high-patience types always reciprocating trust. We also assume that the signaling costs are sufficient to deter low-patience signalers in and of themselves (k>δL bL); that is, even in the absence of social benefits coming from not sending the signal (i.e., attracting the trust of hightrust choosers in the aversive signaling equilibrium).

Reputations

The signaler has two observable attributes: their signaling decision (sent or did not send, fixed after Phase 1), and their trust game reputation, reflecting their last reciprocation decision: good if they last reciprocated, bad if they last defected, unknown if they have never been trusted. The chooser observes both when deciding whether to extend trust.

Strategies

A chooser strategy specifies what level of cooperation to initially choose, as a function of their type (high-trust or low-trust) and the signaler's initial signaling decision (sent or did not send); and whether to extend trust, as a function of their type, the level of cooperation, and the signaler's full reputation. A signaler strategy specifies whether to send the signal, as a function of their type (high-, medium-, or low-patience), and whether to reciprocate trust, as a function of their type, the level of cooperation, and their current reputation.

Equilibrium analysis

We study Perfect Bayesian Equilibria in pure strategies (Fudenberg & Tirole, 1991). PBE is the standard solution concept for sequential games with incomplete information, and aligns with evolutionary simulations in related settings (Hoffman et al., 2018; Lie-Panis & Hilbe, 2026).

We focus on the following strategy profile, which we call the aversive signaling equilibrium: (1) Medium-patience signalers initially send the signal, low and high-patience signalers do not send.

(2) When faced with a sender, both high and low-trust choosers set the level of cooperation at low and extend trust. When faced with a non-sender, high-trust choosers set the level of cooperation at high and extend trust, while low-trust choosers set the level of cooperation at low and distrust. (3) Subsequently, all choosers trust based on trust game reputation only, trusting signalers with good reputation and distrusting those with bad reputation regardless of initial signaling decision. Signaler reciprocation behavior is a function of own type and cooperation level, as detailed above.

We derive five conditions that are jointly necessary and sufficient for the aversive signaling equilibrium to exist (Supplementary Note 1, conditions 3.3-3.7).

Numerical solution.

To characterize the equilibrium domain (Figure 2. C.), we adopt a binomial parametrization that reduces both signaler and chooser types distributions to a single parameter μ∈(0,1), capturing both the level of patience and trust in the shared population: pH=qH=μ², pM=2μ(1-μ), pL=qL=(1-μ)². We assume symmetric payoffs (γl = cl, βl = bl) and fix the high-level surplus at bH-cH = s(bL-cL), with s = 3/2. We evaluate the five equilibrium conditions on a grid over μ and cH/bH. Other parameters: δ=(1/8, 1/2, 7/8), cL=1/3, bL=1, r=7/10, k=1/4.

Study 3

Dataset and participants

We reanalyzed the cross-national dataset of Sorokowski et al. (2023): 9,474 participants from 45 countries, aged 15 to 99, who were in a romantic relationship (dating, engaged, or married; 123 participants of the analytic sample did not report the type of relationship). Participants completed the 45-item version of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale and reported their age, gender, relationship length, and economic situation. Countries were matched to their HDI after harmonizing the seven country names spelled differently in the survey and in the United Nations Development Programme, 2022 table (e.g., Turkey and Türkiye), so that all 45 countries entered the analysis. We excluded 682 participants without information on gender, age, or economic situation (18, 40 and 624, each participant being counted under the first missing variable in this order). The analytic sample comprised 8,792 participants (38 to 826 per country; 72 of them aged 15 to 17) and 388,840 item-level responses. Item non-response was 1.7% (6,800 of 395,640 possible responses; 7,495 participants answered all 45 items). It was concentrated in few participants: 206 had no answer to items 25 to 34, one block of the questionnaire, including 133 of the 309 participants in Vietnam and 53 of the 154 in China. Missing responses were left out, and the participant's other responses kept.

Measures

Romantic love was assessed using the 45-item version of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale. Each item was rated on a scale from 1 to 9. Rather than aggregating items into composite scores, we analyzed responses at the item level to preserve theoretically relevant variation.

Four coders rated the extent to which each item implies partner idealization: three authors of this paper (VT, NB and CC) and a research assistant who did not know the hypothesis (NR). None of them had seen the responses to the items when rating them. All of them were asked to rate "the extent to which somebody agreeing with this statement implies partner idealization in a romantic relationship, whether knowingly or unknowingly, voluntarily or involuntarily". The four ratings were averaged and rescaled to [0, 1] to form a single item-level PI score (M = 0.36, SD = 0.28). The reliability of the averaged rating was high (ICC(2,k) = 0.875, 95% CI [0.76, 0.93], twoway random, absolute agreement); that of a single coder was 0.64 (ICC(2,1)). Coders differed in how they used the scale (from 0 to 28 of the 45 items rated 0), but leaving out any one coder changed the scores little (correlations of 0.98 or more with the four-coder scores) and left the results unchanged (Supplementary Note 4).

Country-level socio-economic conditions were indexed using the Human Development Index (HDI) of 2021 (United Nations Development Programme, 2022). Individual-level socioeconomic status (SES) was participants' self-rated economic situation, on a scale from 1 to 5.

Statistical analysis

The analysis and decision rules were pre-registered. Observation ij (participant i, item j) was modelled as: with random intercepts ui (participant), vj (item) and wi (country of participant i).

The outcome and the continuous predictors were z-scored over the item-level responses of the analytic sample, and the squared terms are squares of these z-scores, so that coefficients are in SD of the outcome per SD of the predictor. The model was fitted by REML with lme4 (1.1-38) and lmerTest (3.1-3) in R 4.5.1. As pre-registered, a prediction was considered supported if the 95% interval of 1,000 bootstrap refits of the model excluded zero. Because HDI varies between countries only, each bootstrap sample drew 45 countries with replacement, each with all its participants, and the intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the refitted coefficients. The pre-registered rule for a singular fit (removing the random effect with the smallest variance until the fit is not singular) was not needed. The two pre-registered focal effects were γ₁ (PI × HDI) and γ₂ (PI × SES); both were predicted to be negative and significant.

The PI × HDI interaction is a cross-level interaction: PI varies between items and HDI between countries. Tested without a random slope of PI across countries, it would treat the item-level responses as independent evidence about a country-level relationship (Heisig & Schaeffer, 2019). We therefore also fitted M1, which adds to M0 correlated random slopes of PI across participants and across countries (optimizer bobyqa), with t-tests on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. M1 was not pre-registered. Supplementary Note 4 reports further checks, none of them pre-registered: a model that also lets the effects of HDI and SES vary across items (M2), the interaction of PI with squared HDI, two-stage analyses, response style, SES within and between countries, leaving out each coder, and interpersonal trust.

Coefficients are reported with 95% intervals and two-tailed tests. Supplementary Table S5 gives every coefficient of M0 and M1, and the scripts (study3_analysis.R, study3_robustness.R, study3_irtree.R and study3_figure3. R) are available on the project OSF repository (https://osf.io/84k6w/).

Study 4

Participants and materials

We analyzed the cross-national survey of Kowal et al. (2025), collected in 2021 (117,293 participants). Country names were harmonized with the HDI table, and six places without an HDI value (Taiwan, Kosovo, Monaco, Somalia, Nauru, and Somaliland; 783 participants) were left out. After restricting to participants with complete responses on country of residence, social class, age, gender, and the infidelity question, the analytic sample comprised 84,382 adults (aged 18 to 90) from 160 countries (1 to 8,466 per country). Participants answered the question "Have you ever been sexually or emotionally unfaithful to a romantic partner?" (1 = yes,0 = no), and 33.5% answered yes. SES was the answer to "Which of the following answers best describes your social class level?" (1 = lower class to5 = upper class). Gender was male, female, nonbinary, or prefer not to say. Country-level human development was the HDI of 2021, the year of data collection (United Nations Development Programme, 2022, as distributed by Our World in Data).

Statistical analysis

At the country level, we computed, for each country of residence, the share of respondents reporting any infidelity, and correlated it with HDI across the 160 countries, without a minimum sample size. We computed this correlation with the same weight for every country and with each country weighted by its number of respondents.

The focal test, though, was at the individual level: we fitted a generalized linear mixed-effects model with a binomial likelihood and a logit link, with reported infidelity as the outcome, standardized HDI, SES, age, and gender as fixed effects, and a random intercept for country of residence:

The model was estimated with lme4::glmer (version 1.1-38, R 4.5.1; Laplace approximation, bobyqa optimizer). Gender entered as a four-level factor, with men as the reference category. Continuous predictors were z-scored so that fixed-effect coefficients are directly interpretable on the standardized log-odds scale, and are also reported as odds ratios per one-standard-deviation increase in the predictor.

We also refitted the model among participants under 65, separately for men and for women, and with the logarithm of GDP per capita (PPP, constant 2021 international dollars; World Bank, 2026) in place of HDI (Supplementary Note 5).

Reporting

This study was not pre-registered. It tests a directional prediction derived from the model. The scripts (study4_analysis.R, study4_robustness.R), including the harmonization of country names, are available on the project OSF repository (https://osf.io/84k6w/).
